title: Blog 1
content:
Uploading to Amazon S3 directly from a web or mobile application Item Detail Original post Uploading to Amazon S3 directly from a web or mobile application Source AWS Compute Blog · James Beswick · 2020 Topic Serverless · Storage Summary The post shows how to let a browser or mobile app upload files straight to Amazon S3 instead of through an application server. The client calls an API Gateway endpoint, Lambda creates a presigned URL valid for 300 seconds with a random object key, and the client sends the file directly to S3. This reduces server load and network traffic; the post also notes that the bucket needs CORS rules and that a JWT authorizer should restrict who can upload.
Relevance to SnapThumb SnapThumb uses exactly this pattern in steps 2–5. One difference: SnapThumb uses a presigned POST instead of a presigned PUT, because POST supports a content-length-range condition so S3 itself rejects files over 10 MB, a limit the original post leaves unaddressed.
Main content The problem with uploading through a server Traditionally the user sends a file to the application server, which stores it temporarily and then moves it to storage. Every file crosses the server twice, using bandwidth and CPU. Apps with seasonal spikes (a holiday greeting app, for example) are most likely to overload exactly when they are busiest.
The idea: separate asking for permission from sending the file The client works in two steps:
Call an API Gateway endpoint. It runs the getSignedURL Lambda function, which asks S3 for a presigned URL and returns it. Send the file straight to S3 with that URL. The backend never handles the file bytes. S3 is highly available and durable, which makes it a good home for user uploads.
The Lambda function that signs the link The object key is random (a random number plus .jpg), so users cannot overwrite each other’s files. The content type is fixed to image/jpeg and the link expires after 300 seconds. The SDK default is 15 minutes; the author suggests the shortest expiry that still works. The function returns JSON with the upload link and the key. Its role only needs permission to write objects (the SAM S3WritePolicy template). Deploying and testing The sample lives in the aws-samples/amazon-s3-presigned-urls-aws-sam repository and deploys with sam deploy --guided. The APIendpoint output plus /uploads is the address that hands out links. Postman test: GET to receive uploadURL, then PUT with the image as the body; S3 answers 200 OK and the file appears in the bucket. Web test: the sample page uses fetch to PUT the file to the link it received. CORS Because the browser sends the request to another domain (S3), the bucket needs CORS rules. The sample allows every origin and header with GET, PUT and HEAD; production should narrow this to the app’s own domain.
Security A second template (templateWithAuth.yaml) attaches a JWT authorizer to the HTTP API. Clients send a token in the Authorization header and API Gateway checks it before calling Lambda. The post uses Auth0 as the example and names Amazon Cognito as an equivalent option. Uploaded objects are private by default. To make them public, set the public-read ACL when signing, and give the function s3:PutObjectAcl. The post’s conclusion Uploading straight to S3 moves the heaviest work out of the application, so it handles traffic spikes without adding servers. The post does not cover multipart uploads or file size limits.

title: Create the API Lambda
content:
Step 1: Create the function Lambda → Create function, name snapthumb-api, Python 3.12, keep Create a new role with basic Lambda permissions → Create function. Replace lambda_function.py with the code below → Deploy. """SnapThumb - hàm Lambda cho API (API Gateway HTTP API, payload 2.0). POST /uploads -> kiểm tra file, tạo bản ghi PENDING, trả về presigned POST để trình duyệt upload thẳng lên S3 GET /images -> danh sách ảnh mới nhất kèm link xem có thời hạn DELETE /images/{id} -> xoá ảnh gốc, thumbnail và bản ghi """ import json import logging import os import uuid from datetime import datetime, timezone from decimal import Decimal import boto3 from botocore.config import Config logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) ALLOWED_TYPES = {"image/jpeg": "jpg", "image/png": "png", "image/webp": "webp"} MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024 UPLOAD_EXPIRES = 300 # giây: link upload hết hạn sau 5 phút VIEW_EXPIRES = 3600 # giây: link xem ảnh hết hạn sau 1 giờ LIST_LIMIT = 50 _s3 = None _table = None def s3(): global _s3 if _s3 is None: region = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "us-east-1") # Endpoint theo region để link upload đi thẳng tới đúng region của bucket. _s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name=region, endpoint_url=f"https://s3.{region}.amazonaws.com", config=Config(signature_version="s3v4", s3={"addressing_style": "virtual"})) return _s3 def table(): global _table if _table is None: _table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table(os.environ["TABLE_NAME"]) return _table def bucket(): return os.environ["BUCKET_NAME"] def _json_default(value): if isinstance(value, Decimal): return int(value) if value == value.to_integral_value() else float(value) raise TypeError(type(value)) def reply(status, payload=None): res = {"statusCode": status, "headers": {"Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8"}} if payload is not None: res["body"] = json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False, default=_json_default) return res def create_upload(event): try: body = json.loads(event.get("body") or "{}") except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError): return reply(400, {"error": "Body must be JSON"}) filename = str(body.get("filename") or "").strip()[:200] content_type = str(body.get("contentType") or "") size = body.get("size") if not filename: return reply(400, {"error": "filename is required"}) if content_type not in ALLOWED_TYPES: return reply(400, {"error": "Only JPEG, PNG and WebP images are allowed"}) if not isinstance(size, int) or size <= 0 or size > MAX_BYTES: return reply(400, {"error": f"File size must be between 1 byte and {MAX_BYTES // (1024 * 1024)} MB"}) image_id = uuid.uuid4().hex key = f"uploads/{image_id}.{ALLOWED_TYPES[content_type]}" table().put_item(Item={ "id": image_id, "filename": filename, "contentType": content_type, "originalKey": key, "status": "PENDING", "createdAt": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), }) upload = s3().generate_presigned_post( Bucket=bucket(), Key=key, Fields={"Content-Type": content_type}, # S3 tự từ chối nếu file sai loại hoặc lớn hơn giới hạn, kể cả khi trình duyệt khai báo sai. Conditions=[{"Content-Type": content_type}, ["content-length-range", 1, MAX_BYTES]], ExpiresIn=UPLOAD_EXPIRES, ) return reply(201, {"id": image_id, "upload": upload}) def view_url(key): return s3().generate_presigned_url("get_object", Params={"Bucket": bucket(), "Key": key}, ExpiresIn=VIEW_EXPIRES) def list_images(event): items, kwargs = [], {} while True: page = table().scan(**kwargs) items.extend(page.get("Items", [])) if "LastEvaluatedKey" not in page or len(items) >= 500: break kwargs["ExclusiveStartKey"] = page["LastEvaluatedKey"] items.sort(key=lambda i: i.get("createdAt", ""), reverse=True) items = items[:LIST_LIMIT] for item in items: if item.get("originalKey"): item["originalUrl"] = view_url(item["originalKey"]) if item.get("thumbKey"): item["thumbUrl"] = view_url(item["thumbKey"]) return reply(200, {"images": items}) def delete_image(event): image_id = (event.get("pathParameters") or {}).get("id", "") item = table().get_item(Key={"id": image_id}).get("Item") if not item: return reply(404, {"error": "Image not found"}) keys = [item[k] for k in ("originalKey", "thumbKey") if item.get(k)] if keys: s3().delete_objects(Bucket=bucket(), Delete={"Objects": [{"Key": k} for k in keys]}) table().delete_item(Key={"id": image_id}) return reply(204) ROUTES = { "POST /uploads": create_upload, "GET /images": list_images, "DELETE /images/{id}": delete_image, } def handler(event, context): route = ROUTES.get(event.get("routeKey", "")) if not route: return reply(404, {"error": "Not found"}) try: return route(event) except Exception: logger.exception("Unhandled error on %s", event.get("routeKey")) return reply(500, {"error": "Internal error"}) lambda_handler = handler # tên hàm mặc định của Lambda console / default handler name in the console What the code does Part Explanation ROUTES Maps API Gateway’s routeKey (e.g. POST /uploads) to a Python function create_upload Checks name, type (JPEG/PNG/WebP) and size (≤ 10 MB), writes PENDING, calls generate_presigned_post Conditions Rules baked into the signature: S3 rejects a file of another type or over 10 MB list_images Reads all items, sorts newest first, adds generate_presigned_url view links lambda_handler = handler Lets the console’s default handler lambda_function.lambda_handler call the code _json_default DynamoDB returns numbers as Decimal; this converts them for JSON item.get(...) in list/delete Records without originalKey or thumbKey (failed or console uploads) are listed and deleted without crashing the whole API Step 2: Configuration Configuration → General configuration → Edit: Memory 256 MB, Timeout 10 sec. Environment variables: TABLE_NAME = snapthumb-images, BUCKET_NAME = snapthumb-images-<your-name>. Step 3: Permissions Add an inline policy snapthumb-api-access to the function’s role:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Metadata", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:Scan", "dynamodb:DeleteItem"], "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:ACCOUNT_ID:table/snapthumb-images" }, { "Sid": "SignUploads", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::snapthumb-images-YOURNAME/uploads/*" }, { "Sid": "SignViewsAndDelete", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::snapthumb-images-YOURNAME/*" } ] } Signing a link makes no call to S3, but the link only works if the signer is allowed to do what the link does. That is why the API role needs s3:PutObject on uploads/* even though it never uploads anything itself.

title: Publish the Pillow Layer
content:
Why a layer Pillow contains compiled code, so it must be built for Lambda’s Linux and Python 3.12, not for your laptop. The command below asks pip for the right Linux wheel.
Build and publish in CloudShell Open CloudShell (the >_ icon at the top of the console), in ap-southeast-1. Run: mkdir -p pillow-layer/python python3 -m pip install --target pillow-layer/python \ --platform manylinux_2_28_x86_64 --platform manylinux2014_x86_64 \ --implementation cp --python-version 3.12 --only-binary=:all: Pillow==11.0.0 cd pillow-layer && zip -qr ../pillow-layer.zip python && cd .. aws lambda publish-layer-version --layer-name pillow-py312 \ --zip-file fileb://pillow-layer.zip \ --compatible-runtimes python3.12 --compatible-architectures x86_64 \ --query LayerVersionArn --output text The last command prints the layer ARN, e.g. arn:aws:lambda:ap-southeast-1:123456789012:layer:pillow-py312:1. A Python layer must put libraries under a python/ folder inside the zip; Lambda adds that folder to the import path.

title: Workshop Overview
content:
How SnapThumb works The system has two Lambda functions with different jobs:
Component AWS service What it does Web page Amazon CloudFront + Amazon S3 (private bucket, Origin Access Control) Serves the page over HTTPS: drag-and-drop upload and a gallery of thumbnails Front door Amazon API Gateway HTTPS endpoints the page calls API Lambda AWS Lambda Validates files, signs time-limited upload and view links, lists and deletes images Image storage Amazon S3 (private bucket) Originals under uploads/, thumbnails under thumbnails/ Thumbnail Lambda AWS Lambda + Pillow Runs automatically for each new image and creates its thumbnail Image records Amazon DynamoDB Status (PENDING → DONE / FAILED), dimensions, sizes, processing time Logs Amazon CloudWatch Every run of both functions Alerts (admin only) CloudWatch alarms + Amazon SNS Email the administrator when the thumbnail function crashes, the API returns 5xx, or many uploads fail The numbers in the diagram follow the data flow: (1) open the web page through CloudFront over HTTPS, (2) POST /uploads, (3) API Gateway calls the API Lambda, (4) it writes a PENDING record and returns a signed link, (5) the browser uploads straight to S3, (6) the ObjectCreated event calls the thumbnail Lambda, (7) it saves the thumbnail in thumbnails/, (8) updates the record to DONE, (9) the page lists images with GET /images. CloudWatch collects logs, metrics and alarms throughout.
Why these services Need Chosen service Why Alternative considered Store originals and thumbnails, notify on new files Amazon S3 Unlimited, cheap storage; built-in Event Notifications start the processing; presigned POST lets the browser upload directly with size and type limits Disk on EC2 / EFS: needs a running server and has no built-in “new file” event Process each image AWS Lambda Runs only when an image arrives, billed per millisecond, scales out automatically when many images arrive at once EC2 or ECS worker: pays 24/7 even when idle, needs scaling and patching HTTPS endpoints for the web page Amazon API Gateway – HTTP API Managed HTTPS, CORS and throttling with no server; cheaper and lower latency than REST API, and SnapThumb needs none of the REST-only features (API keys, request validation, direct AWS WAF integration) REST API (more features, higher price); ALB + EC2 (always-on cost) Store each image’s status and details Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand) Simple key–value access by id, millisecond latency, no server or connection pool to manage from Lambda, pay per request Amazon RDS: always-on instance cost, schema and database connections from Lambda to manage Logs, metrics and alerts Amazon CloudWatch Lambda and API Gateway send logs and metrics automatically; metric filters turn log lines into metrics; alarms watch them Third-party monitoring: extra cost and agents Serve the web page securely Amazon CloudFront + Origin Access Control HTTPS with an AWS certificate, edge caching, and the web bucket stays private: only this distribution can read it S3 static website endpoint: HTTP only and the bucket must be public Send alert emails Amazon SNS An alarm can publish to an SNS topic with no code; email subscription needs only a confirmation click Amazon SES: requires verifying a sender identity and writing code Permissions AWS IAM One role per function with only the actions and resources it needs; no access keys in code Shared admin role (violates least privilege) Build and delete everything AWS CloudFormation Whole system as one template; same result every time; one command deletes everything so nothing keeps costing money; runs in CloudShell with no extra tools AWS CDK / Terraform: need extra tooling and a build step Security in the design Risk What SnapThumb does Someone reads other people’s images The image bucket blocks all public access; images are only shown through presigned links that expire after 1 hour AWS keys leak No access keys in code or in the browser; each Lambda function runs with its own IAM role Permissions too broad Each role has only the actions it needs, scoped to the table and to a prefix: the thumbnail function can only read uploads/*, write thumbnails/* and call UpdateItem Malicious or oversized uploads The API checks type and size; the presigned POST carries Content-Type and content-length-range conditions so S3 itself rejects other files; upload links expire after 5 minutes; Pillow checks the real file content API abuse Throttling of 10 requests/s (burst 20) on the HTTP API Someone reads or changes the web page files in S3 The web bucket blocks all public access; only the CloudFront distribution can read it (Origin Access Control, policy condition on the distribution ARN) Data intercepted in transit Every connection is HTTPS: CloudFront redirects HTTP to HTTPS, API Gateway and presigned S3 links use HTTPS only Data at rest S3 encrypts objects (SSE-S3, AES-256) and DynamoDB encrypts the table by default Problems go unnoticed CloudWatch alarms email the administrator through SNS (5.8) Known gap for a demo: the API has no sign-in, so anyone with the link can upload and delete. 5.8 lists how to close it (Amazon Cognito). The web page itself is served over HTTPS by CloudFront, and both buckets block all public access.
Scalability Amazon S3 stores any number of images, and browsers upload straight to it, so the API never carries image data and does not become a bottleneck. AWS Lambda runs one invocation per image and runs them in parallel: in the test, 6 images uploaded at once were processed by 5 instances at the same time. The limit is the account’s Lambda concurrency in the region (see Service Quotas). Amazon DynamoDB on-demand adjusts throughput automatically; no capacity planning. At larger scale, GET /images should stop scanning the whole table (see Limitations and next steps in 5.8). Key concepts Event-driven architecture Nothing polls the bucket. When an object is created, S3 emits an event and invokes the Lambda function directly. The function runs only when there is work, and AWS runs many copies in parallel when many images arrive.
S3 Event Notifications A bucket setting that says “when an object is created under this prefix, call this target”. SnapThumb listens only to uploads/. Thumbnails are written to thumbnails/, so writing a thumbnail never triggers the function again. Without this split, the function would trigger itself in an endless loop.
Presigned URL / presigned POST A link signed with the API Lambda’s permissions that lets the browser upload one specific object directly to S3 for a short time (5 minutes). The browser never gets AWS credentials, and large files never pass through Lambda. The presigned POST also carries conditions: S3 rejects files that are not the declared type or are larger than 10 MB.
Lambda layer A zip of libraries shared by functions. Pillow (the Python imaging library) is not included in the Lambda runtime, so you publish it once as a layer and attach it to the Thumbnail function.
DynamoDB on-demand A NoSQL table billed per request, with no capacity to plan. Each image is one item keyed by id.
CloudFront and Origin Access Control (OAC) CloudFront is AWS’s content delivery network: it serves files over HTTPS from edge locations near the user and caches them. With OAC, CloudFront signs every request it sends to S3, and the bucket policy allows only that distribution. The bucket stays private, yet the page is public through the CloudFront link.
Metric filter and alarm A metric filter counts log lines that match a pattern (for example Failed to process) and publishes the count as a CloudWatch metric. An alarm watches a metric and, when it crosses a threshold, sends a message to an Amazon SNS topic, which emails the subscribers.
Test each part before moving on: upload a file to the bucket by hand and check that a thumbnail appears (5.5) → call the API with curl (5.6) → use the web page (5.7).

title: Blog 2
content:
Resize Images on the Fly with Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, and Amazon API Gateway Item Detail Original post Resize Images on the Fly with Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, and Amazon API Gateway Source AWS Compute Blog · John Pignata · 2017 Topic Serverless · Image processing Summary The post shows how to resize images on demand. Originals are stored in S3; when a user requests a size that does not exist yet, an S3 redirect rule sends the request to API Gateway, Lambda downloads the original, resizes it, saves it to S3 and redirects the user to the new file. Later requests are served straight from S3.
Relevance to SnapThumb This post helps compare two designs. The original creates images when someone views them (lazy), which suits many different sizes. SnapThumb creates them on upload (eager) through S3 events, which suits one fixed size that should be ready immediately. This comparison feeds the risk and future-work parts of the report.
Main content Eager or lazy processing The common approach is eager processing: whenever a new image arrives, an S3 event calls Lambda to create every size up front. The post proposes lazy processing: a size is created only the first time someone asks for it. The author gives three benefits:
Faster design changes: adding a new size does not require reprocessing the whole image archive. Lower storage cost: sizes nobody uses are never created; lifecycle rules can expire old resized files. Better resilience: if one resize fails, the next request retries it instead of the image staying broken for everyone. How one request flows The browser asks the bucket’s website endpoint for a resized image. The image does not exist yet, so S3 sends a temporary redirect to the API. The browser follows the redirect to API Gateway. API Gateway invokes the Lambda function. Lambda downloads the original, resizes it and saves it to the bucket under the requested key. API Gateway permanently redirects the browser to the new file in S3. From then on S3 serves the image directly. If the file is deleted, the cycle repeats. The S3 redirect rule The bucket has static website hosting and a routing rule: on a 404 error, redirect (code 307, temporary) to the API hostname, turning the path into the key parameter of the resize function. A 307 keeps browsers from remembering the redirect, because once the image exists S3 can serve it.
Setup steps Bucket: allow public read, enable static website hosting, note the endpoint. Lambda: a function named resize with an open API Gateway trigger and code from function.zip in the serverless-image-resizing repository. Memory 1536 MB, timeout 10 seconds. The role only needs CloudWatch Logs and s3:PutObject on the bucket. Environment variables: BUCKET (bucket name) and URL (the bucket’s website endpoint). Testing: upload the sample image, then open sizes such as 300x300, 25x25 and 500x500; check CloudWatch Logs if something fails. Notes for production The post’s version is a simplified example. Production needs an allowed-sizes list, otherwise anyone can request endless sizes and fill the bucket. Keep resized images in a separate bucket so lifecycle rules can apply to them. A 2018 update recommends the AWS Serverless Image Handler solution for production. General serverless benefits: no servers to patch or scale, and no capacity to over-provision.

title: Create the Function and S3 Trigger
content:
Step 1: Create the function AWS Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch. Name: snapthumb-thumbnail, Runtime: Python 3.12, Architecture: x86_64. Permissions: keep Create a new role with basic Lambda permissions. Lambda creates the role snapthumb-thumbnail-role-…, which can already write logs to CloudWatch; Step 3 adds S3 and DynamoDB access. → Create function. Replace lambda_function.py with the code below → Deploy. """SnapThumb - hàm Lambda tạo ảnh thu nhỏ. Kích hoạt bởi sự kiện S3 ObjectCreated trên tiền tố uploads/. Đọc ảnh gốc, tạo thumbnail JPEG (cạnh dài tối đa THUMB_MAX_SIZE px), ghi vào thumbnails/, rồi cập nhật trạng thái và thông số vào DynamoDB. """ import io import logging import os import urllib.parse from datetime import datetime, timezone import boto3 from PIL import Image, ImageOps logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) UPLOAD_PREFIX = "uploads/" THUMB_PREFIX = "thumbnails/" THUMB_MAX_SIZE = int(os.environ.get("THUMB_MAX_SIZE", "320")) JPEG_QUALITY = 85 _s3 = None _table = None def s3(): global _s3 if _s3 is None: _s3 = boto3.client("s3") return _s3 def table(): global _table if _table is None: _table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table(os.environ["TABLE_NAME"]) return _table def make_thumbnail(data, max_size=THUMB_MAX_SIZE): """Trả về (bytes JPEG của thumbnail, (rộng, cao) gốc, (rộng, cao) thumbnail).""" with Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)) as original: img = ImageOps.exif_transpose(original) # xoay đúng chiều theo EXIF của ảnh điện thoại original_size = img.size if img.mode in ("RGBA", "LA") or (img.mode == "P" and "transparency" in img.info): # JPEG không có kênh trong suốt: đặt ảnh lên nền trắng rgba = img.convert("RGBA") img = Image.new("RGB", rgba.size, (255, 255, 255)) img.paste(rgba, mask=rgba.split()[-1]) elif img.mode not in ("RGB", "L"): img = img.convert("RGB") img.thumbnail((max_size, max_size), Image.LANCZOS) # title: Proposal
content:
SnapThumb An automatic image thumbnail service on AWS 1. Executive Summary SnapThumb is a web app where users upload images and get thumbnails back within seconds. It follows an event-driven architecture: as soon as an image lands in Amazon S3, S3 emits an event and AWS Lambda runs automatically to create the thumbnail, with no server running all the time. The whole system is serverless, and the demo costs close to 0 USD per month.
2. Problem Statement Current Problem Phone photos are often 3–8 MB and 4000 px or more wide. Showing originals in lists, galleries or product pages makes pages slow and wastes bandwidth, especially on mobile networks. Resizing on an always-on server means paying for it when nobody uploads, and handling bursts yourself. Solution Users upload images directly from the browser to Amazon S3 with a time-limited link (presigned POST). S3 triggers AWS Lambda for each new image; Lambda uses Pillow to create a 320 px thumbnail and stores it back in S3. Image details (status, dimensions, size, processing time) are written to Amazon DynamoDB for the UI. Benefits Thumbnails are about 90–98% smaller than originals, so pages load faster. Pay only when images are processed; idle cost is close to zero. Scales automatically: 1 or 100 images at once, Lambda runs them in parallel. New processing steps (compression, watermarking, detection) can be added without touching the upload path. Target users Developers and small teams building web or mobile apps with many user-uploaded images (class or club photo galleries, online shops, profile pictures in a student management system) who need thumbnails without running servers. End users: people who upload and view images on the web page. Administrators: whoever deploys and operates the system and receives alert emails when something goes wrong. Goals and success criteria Expected outputs: (1) a web page to upload, view and delete images; (2) an HTTP API with three routes; (3) automatic thumbnails in S3 with a record in DynamoDB; (4) logs, metrics and three alarms that email the administrator; (5) a CloudFormation template that creates and deletes the whole system with one command.
Criterion Target Measured on AWS Time from upload to finished thumbnail 1–3 seconds 1.1–2.8 seconds including cold start; 0.48 seconds of function time when warm Thumbnail size versus a phone photo At least 90% smaller 99.8% smaller (6.1 MB → 12.7 KB) Handling bad input No hang, clear error Fake image → FAILED; GIF or declared 11 MB → 400; sending 10.5 MB → S3 returns 400 EntityTooLarge Alerts Administrator emailed within 5 minutes Alarm fired after 71 seconds, email delivered Rebuilding the infrastructure One command deploy.sh creates 26 resources; destroy.sh removes everything Cost Under 1 USD/month for 1,000 images Estimated under 0.20 USD/month (section 6) Fit with the FCAJ program SnapThumb uses the program’s core services (Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon DynamoDB, AWS IAM, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudFormation) and applies the serverless, event-driven pattern for file processing instead of a web application on an always-on server.
3. Solution Architecture Solution Architecture Main flow (1–9):
The user loads the static web page from Amazon S3. The page sends POST /uploads (file name, type, size) to Amazon API Gateway. API Gateway invokes the API Lambda. The API Lambda validates the file, writes a PENDING record to DynamoDB and returns an upload link valid for 5 minutes. The browser uploads the image directly to S3, under uploads/. S3 emits an ObjectCreated event and invokes the Thumbnail Lambda. The Thumbnail Lambda reads the original, creates the thumbnail and stores it under thumbnails/. The Thumbnail Lambda updates the DynamoDB record to DONE with dimensions, sizes and processing time. The page calls GET /images every 1.5 seconds; once the image is done, the API Lambda returns view links valid for 1 hour and the thumbnail appears. Monitoring and security: both Lambda functions log to Amazon CloudWatch, and three CloudWatch alarms email the team through Amazon SNS when the thumbnail function crashes, the API returns server errors, or many uploads fail. Each function has its own IAM role with only the permissions it needs. The image bucket is not public.
AWS Services Used Service Layer Role Amazon CloudFront + Amazon S3 (web bucket, private) Frontend Serves the static web UI over HTTPS; Origin Access Control keeps the bucket private Amazon API Gateway API HTTPS endpoints POST /uploads, GET /images, DELETE /images/{id}; CORS; throttling AWS Lambda (API) Backend Validates files, signs time-limited upload/view links, lists and deletes images Amazon S3 (image bucket) Backend Stores originals (uploads/) and thumbnails (thumbnails/); emits events on new images AWS Lambda (Thumbnail) Backend Creates thumbnails with Pillow Amazon DynamoDB Backend Stores each image’s status and details Amazon CloudWatch Monitoring Logs, metrics, a metric filter and 3 alarms Amazon SNS Monitoring Emails the team when an alarm fires AWS IAM Security Least-privilege permissions per function AWS CloudFormation Deployment Creates and deletes all infrastructure from code Why these services Need Chosen service Why Alternative considered Store originals and thumbnails, notify on new files Amazon S3 Unlimited, cheap storage; built-in Event Notifications start the processing; presigned POST lets the browser upload directly with size and type limits Disk on EC2 / EFS: needs a running server and has no built-in “new file” event Process each image AWS Lambda Runs only when an image arrives, billed per millisecond, scales out automatically when many images arrive at once EC2 or ECS worker: pays 24/7 even when idle, needs scaling and patching HTTPS endpoints for the web page Amazon API Gateway – HTTP API Managed HTTPS, CORS and throttling with no server; cheaper and lower latency than REST API, and SnapThumb needs none of the REST-only features (API keys, request validation) REST API (more features, higher price); ALB + EC2 (always-on cost) Store each image’s status and details Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand) Simple key–value access by id, millisecond latency, no server or connection pool to manage from Lambda, pay per request Amazon RDS: always-on instance cost, schema and database connections from Lambda to manage Logs, metrics and alerts Amazon CloudWatch Lambda and API Gateway send logs and metrics automatically; metric filters turn log lines into metrics; alarms watch them Third-party monitoring: extra cost and agents Send alert emails Amazon SNS An alarm can publish to an SNS topic with no code; email subscription needs only a confirmation click Amazon SES: requires verifying a sender identity and writing code Permissions AWS IAM One role per function with only the actions and resources it needs; no access keys in code Shared admin role (violates least privilege) Build and delete everything AWS CloudFormation Whole system as one template; same result every time; one command deletes everything so nothing keeps costing money; runs in CloudShell with no extra tools AWS CDK / Terraform: need extra tooling and a build step Component Design Frontend A single plain index.html (HTML, CSS, JavaScript): drag-and-drop for multiple images, gallery, per-image status. Checks file type (JPEG, PNG, WebP) and size (up to 10 MB) before upload. Backend API Lambda (Python 3.12): three routes; issues presigned POSTs with conditions on file type and size, so S3 itself rejects invalid files. Thumbnail Lambda (Python 3.12 + Pillow): keeps the aspect ratio, honours EXIF rotation, flattens transparent PNGs onto white, never enlarges small images, outputs JPEG at quality 85. Originals and thumbnails live under different prefixes; the trigger listens only to uploads/, so there is no infinite loop. Data DynamoDB, partition key id, on-demand capacity. Each image stores file name, status (PENDING, DONE, FAILED), dimensions and sizes before/after, and processing time. Security The image bucket blocks all public access; images are viewable only through time-limited links. The web bucket is also private: only the CloudFront distribution can read it (Origin Access Control), and visitors always get HTTPS. Upload links expire after 5 minutes and are limited to 10 MB and allowed types. API Gateway is throttled to 10 requests per second. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases Prepare the account, region and cost alerts. Create the image bucket, DynamoDB table and Pillow layer. Create the Thumbnail Lambda and S3 trigger. Create the API Lambda and API Gateway. Write and host the web UI. Automate with CloudFormation; test, monitor, clean up. Technical Requirements Programming Languages Python 3.12 (Lambda) HTML, CSS, JavaScript (UI) Libraries boto3 (included in Lambda), Pillow 11 (image processing), moto (mocked AWS for tests) Tools AWS Management Console, AWS CloudShell, AWS CLI, Visual Studio Code, Git, Hugo 5. Timeline & Milestones Week Work 1–5 AWS fundamentals: IAM, VPC, EC2, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, Lambda, API Gateway 6 Event-driven architecture, choosing the project, writing the proposal 7 Image bucket, DynamoDB, Pillow packaging 8 Thumbnail Lambda and S3 trigger 9 API Lambda, API Gateway and web UI 10 Automation with CloudFormation; testing 11 Write the workshop; publish the report on GitHub Pages 12 Demo, cleanup, wrap-up 6. Budget Estimation Infrastructure Cost Estimate Assumptions: ap-southeast-1; 1,000 images/month of about 3 MB each; each image viewed about 20 times.
Item Estimated cost (USD/month) Amazon S3 (about 3 GB originals + thumbnails, requests) ~0.08 AWS Lambda (1,000 thumbnails × ~1 s × 1 GB, plus API calls) ~0.00 (Free Tier) Amazon DynamoDB on-demand (tens of thousands of reads/writes) ~0.01 Amazon API Gateway HTTP API (about 25,000 requests) ~0.03 Amazon CloudFront (web page, well under 1 TB / 10 million requests) ~0.00 (Free Tier) Amazon CloudWatch Logs ~0.00 (Free Tier) Amazon CloudWatch alarms (3) + metric filter, Amazon SNS email ~0.00 (Free Tier) Total < 0.20 Cost Control Guidelines Create a 5 USD AWS Budget from day one. Delete all resources after the demo with destroy.sh (section 5.10). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Risk Likelihood Impact Mitigation Infinite loop: Lambda writes to the bucket and triggers itself Medium High Trigger listens only to uploads/; thumbnails go to thumbnails/ Malicious or oversized uploads Medium Medium Presigned POST limits type and size to 10 MB; Lambda marks unreadable files FAILED User images exposed Low High Private bucket; view links expire after 1 hour Unexpected charges Low Medium AWS Budgets, API throttling, cleanup after the demo Missing service quota on a new account Low High Use only core services; check quotas before choosing an architecture 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Outcomes A working web app: upload multiple images, get thumbnails in 1–3 seconds, view and delete them. Logs, metrics and alert emails to the administrator when something goes wrong. Thumbnails at least 90% smaller than phone photos. All infrastructure rebuilt with one command; automated tests included. Practical Value Applies to any image-heavy system: galleries, online shops, profile photos in a student management system. A foundation for further image-processing steps using the same event-driven pattern.

title: Self-evaluation
content:
When I joined the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program, I knew very little about AWS: I had only created an account, a database and an IAM user. After 12 weeks I had built a serverless application on my own using Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon API Gateway and Amazon CloudWatch, and turned it into a workshop others can follow.

title: Host the Web Frontend (S3 + CloudFront)
content:
The page is stored in a private S3 bucket and served over HTTPS by Amazon CloudFront. CloudFront reads the bucket through Origin Access Control (OAC), so nobody can open the bucket directly: the only way in is the CloudFront link.
Browser ──HTTPS──► CloudFront ──(OAC, signed request)──► S3 web bucket (private) Step 1: Private website bucket S3 → Create bucket snapthumb-web-<your-name>, same Region as the rest of the lab. Keep Block all public access ticked (the default) and create the bucket. Do not turn on Static website hosting; CloudFront does that job. Step 2: Upload the page Download the source package snapthumb.zip and take web/index.html from it. Create config.js next to it with your Invoke URL: window.SNAPTHUMB_CONFIG = { apiUrl: "https://abc123.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com" }; Upload both files to the root of the bucket. Step 3: CloudFront distribution with OAC CloudFront → Create distribution. If the console asks for a pricing plan, pick the free plan or Pay as you go; either works for this lab. Origin: choose Amazon S3 and pick the bucket snapthumb-web-<your-name> from the list (the REST endpoint, not an s3-website address). Origin access: choose Origin access control settings (recommended) and create a new OAC with the default settings (Sign requests). In the newer console this is the option Allow private S3 bucket access to CloudFront. Default cache behavior: Viewer protocol policy = Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, allowed methods GET, HEAD, cache policy CachingOptimized. Settings: Default root object = index.html. WAF is not needed for this lab. Create the distribution. If the console offers to update the bucket policy for you, accept. Otherwise copy the policy it shows into S3 → bucket → Permissions → Bucket policy. It looks like this: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowCloudFrontOnly", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::snapthumb-web-YOURNAME/*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::ACCOUNT_ID:distribution/DISTRIBUTION_ID" } } } ] } Wait until Last modified shows a date instead of Deploying (about 5 minutes), then open https://<distribution-domain>.cloudfront.net. Why the extra step? A public bucket lets anyone list or download objects straight from S3, and the S3 website endpoint only speaks plain HTTP. With CloudFront + OAC the bucket stays fully private, the page gets HTTPS with an AWS certificate, and files are cached at edge locations close to the user. The AWS:SourceArn condition means only your distribution can read the bucket.
CloudFront caches files. After you upload a new index.html or config.js, open CloudFront → distribution → Invalidations → Create invalidation, enter /*, and reload the page. The deploy.sh script does this for you. If the page shows AccessDenied, check the bucket policy (distribution ID) and that Default root object is index.html.
Check: https://<distribution-domain>.cloudfront.net opens the page with a padlock, while the bucket URL https://snapthumb-web-<your-name>.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html returns AccessDenied.
How the page uses the API For each chosen file it calls POST /uploads and receives upload.url and upload.fields. It builds a FormData with every field, then the file last (S3 requires this order), and posts it to upload.url. It calls GET /images every 1.5 seconds while any image is PENDING, and shows the thumbnail when it turns DONE. Without config.js the page runs in demo mode and shrinks images in the browser. The badge at the top says which mode you are in.

title: Testing and Monitoring
content:
Functional tests # Test Expected 1 Upload a phone photo (JPEG) DONE within a few seconds, thumbnail 320 px on the long edge 2 Upload a portrait photo Thumbnail is upright and taller than wide 3 Upload a transparent PNG Thumbnail has a white background 4 Upload 5 images at once All five finish; Lambda runs them in parallel 5 Upload a .txt renamed to .png Card shows FAILED with the error 6 Choose a 12 MB image Page refuses it before upload 7 Delete an image Card disappears; both files are gone from S3 Measurements Measured on AWS (ap-southeast-1, 18/11/2026). Six test images were uploaded at the same time from a client that uses the API and presigned POST exactly like the web page.
Image Original Thumbnail File size Saved Processing time Landscape JPEG 4032×3024 320×240 6.1 MB → 12.7 KB 99.8% 2,686 ms Portrait JPEG (EXIF rotate 90°) 3000×4000 240×320, upright 5.4 MB → 12.5 KB 99.8% 2,778 ms Transparent PNG 1200×1200 320×320, white background 11.4 KB → 5.2 KB 53.9% 2,547 ms WebP 1920×1080 320×180 818 KB → 16.4 KB 98.0% 2,763 ms Small JPEG 200×150 200×150 (not enlarged) 21.0 KB → 14.9 KB 29.1% 1,076 ms Text file renamed .png – – – – FAILED: cannot identify image file Cold start vs warm. The times above include S3 event delivery and a cold start: the first run of each Lambda instance spends about 0.4 s loading Python and Pillow (Init Duration in the log). On an instance that is already warm, a 6 MB photo took 0.48 s of function time. Peak memory was 213 MB out of 1024 MB; the extra memory is kept because Lambda gives more CPU with more memory.
Other check Result API rejects GIF / declared size 11 MB 400 Client declares 1 KB but sends 10.5 MB S3 refuses: 400 EntityTooLarge CORS preflight OPTIONS /uploads 204, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * Image uploaded straight to S3 (step 5.5) then GET /images 200, image listed; DELETE → 204, both files removed Repeat the table with your own phone photos: the page shows the size, savings and processing time on each card.
Monitoring Lambda → snapthumb-thumbnail → Monitor: invocations, duration, errors. CloudWatch → Log groups → /aws/lambda/snapthumb-thumbnail: one log line per image with sizes before and after. Log groups that Lambda creates by itself never expire. If you built by hand, select both /aws/lambda/snapthumb-… groups → Actions → Edit retention setting(s) → 2 weeks, so logs do not pile up (the CloudFormation template already sets 14 days). CloudFront → Monitoring (or View metrics on the distribution page): requests, data transferred and the share of 4xx/5xx errors for the web page. Alerts (CloudWatch alarms + Amazon SNS) Watching the Monitor tab only works while someone is looking at it. Three alarms send an email as soon as something goes wrong.
Who receives the alerts: only the administrator / operator of the system, i.e. the person who deployed SnapThumb, not the people who upload images. The purpose is to let the admin notice and fix problems (a crashing function, server errors, abuse with fake files) without watching the console all day. End users never receive these emails and cannot subscribe themselves.
The recipient is the email given when deploying (ALARM_EMAIL) or subscribed by hand to the SNS topic. Whoever follows this workshop uses their own email. To add another admin (for example a mentor or teammate): Amazon SNS → Topics → the alarm topic → Create subscription → Email. That person must click Confirm subscription before receiving anything, so nobody is added without agreeing. Alarm Metric Fires when What it catches snapthumb-thumbnail-errors AWS/Lambda → Errors of the thumbnail function ≥ 1 in 5 minutes Crash, timeout or out-of-memory in the thumbnail function snapthumb-api-5xx AWS/ApiGateway → 5xx of the HTTP API ≥ 1 in 5 minutes The API Lambda failed and users see “Internal error” snapthumb-failed-images SnapThumb → FailedImages (metric filter on the log line Failed to process) ≥ 3 in 5 minutes Many corrupt or fake image files at once (abuse or a broken client) The thumbnail function catches bad files and marks them FAILED, so the built-in Errors metric stays at 0 for them. The metric filter counts those log lines and turns them into the FailedImages metric.
With CloudFormation (5.9) The template already contains the SNS topic, the metric filter and the three alarms. Pass your email when deploying, then click Confirm subscription in the email from AWS:
ALARM_EMAIL=you@example.com bash deploy.sh By hand in the console Amazon SNS → Topics → Create topic: type Standard, name snapthumb-alarms. Then Create subscription: protocol Email, your address. Confirm the email. CloudWatch → Log groups → /aws/lambda/snapthumb-thumbnail → Metric filters → Create metric filter: pattern "Failed to process", namespace SnapThumb, metric name FailedImages, metric value 1, default value 0. CloudWatch → Alarms → Create alarm three times, using the table above: statistic Sum, period 5 minutes, condition Greater/Equal, notification to snapthumb-alarms for both In alarm and OK. Under Missing data treatment choose Treat missing data as good (not breaching threshold). Test the alert Upload three fake images (text files renamed to .png) on the web page. Within a few minutes snapthumb-failed-images turns In alarm and the email arrives; when no new failures arrive it returns to OK and a second email confirms it.
Result on AWS (ap-southeast-1, 22/11/2026): three fake images were uploaded; snapthumb-failed-images went from OK to In alarm after 71 seconds, and CloudWatch reported Successfully executed action on the SNS topic, which delivered the email. With no new failures it returned to OK 15 minutes later and sent the second email.

check the spam folder An “OK” alert email right after creating the alarms Each alarm moves from Insufficient data to OK once Normal, nothing to do The CloudFront link shows AccessDenied Bucket policy is missing or has the wrong distribution ID, or Default root object is empty Copy the policy again from the distribution’s Origins → Edit page; set Default root object to index.html (5.7) The page still shows the old version or the demo mode badge CloudFront serves the cached files Invalidations → Create invalidation → /*, then reload; check that config.js is in the bucket The distribution stays at Deploying A new or changed distribution takes a few minutes to reach every edge location Wait 5–10 minutes The console shows no table, function or alarm Another region is selected Choose Asia Pacific (Singapore) at the top right (S3 lists buckets from every region, other services do not) Challenges and solutions Challenge What happened Solution Lesson Project idea blocked by quota The first idea (a chatbot on Amazon Bedrock) could not run because the new account’s quota was too low Switched to SnapThumb, which uses only core services with generous limits Check service quotas before choosing an architecture Risk of an infinite loop The thumbnail function writes to the same bucket that triggers it Trigger only on the uploads/ prefix and write to thumbnails/ Separate input and output prefixes (or buckets) for S3-triggered Lambda Circular dependency in CloudFormation The bucket needs the Lambda permission, and the permission needs the bucket ARN Build the bucket name from the stack name and account ID, and make the bucket depend on the permission Use predictable names to break cycles Pillow does not run on Lambda when installed on a laptop Wheels built for Windows or macOS do not load on Amazon Linux pip install --platform manylinux… --python-version 3.12 --only-binary=:all: in CloudShell Package native libraries for the Lambda runtime and architecture Bug found only on real AWS An image uploaded from the S3 console had no record from the API, so GET /images crashed with a 500 Fill missing fields with if_not_exists, read optional fields with .get(), add 2 regression tests Mocks pass only what you thought of; test end to end on the real service Website bucket had to be public The first version used the S3 static website endpoint: HTTP only, and the bucket needed a public policy Moved to CloudFront + Origin Access Control in two stack updates (first add the distribution next to the public site, test it, then lock the bucket), so the site never went offline Keep buckets private and put CloudFront in front; change live systems in small, tested steps Users lying about file size The browser declares the size; a client could send a bigger file content-length-range in the presigned POST policy: S3 itself rejects files over 10 MB (400 EntityTooLarge) Enforce limits on the server side, not only in the UI Limitations and next steps SnapThumb is a demo. These are known limitations and how AWS services would address them:
Limitation Risk Next step The API has no sign-in Anyone who knows the API address can list and delete every image Add an Amazon Cognito user pool and a JWT authorizer on the HTTP API; store userId with each image No firewall in front of the website and API Bots can use up the API’s throttling limit (real users then get 429) or flood the page Attach AWS WAF rate-based rules to the CloudFront distribution. HTTP APIs cannot use WAF directly, so also route the API through CloudFront (for example a /api/* behavior) or switch to a REST API GET /images scans the whole table Gets slower and costlier as images grow Add a GSI on createdAt (or per-user key) and use Query with pagination A failed thumbnail is not retried A temporary error leaves the image FAILED Configure an on-failure destination / SQS dead-letter queue and retry

title: Automate with CloudFormation
content:
Everything in 5.3–5.7 can be created by one template. This is Infrastructure as Code: the system is described in a file, so it can be rebuilt identically, reviewed and versioned.
What the template contains infra/template.yaml in the source package creates: the image bucket (CORS, S3 trigger), the DynamoDB table, both Lambda functions with their IAM roles and log groups, the HTTP API with three routes and throttling, the private website bucket behind a CloudFront distribution with Origin Access Control, and the alerts (an SNS topic with an optional email subscription, a metric filter and three CloudWatch alarms). Its parameters:
Parameter Default Meaning ThumbnailMaxSize 320 Longest edge of a thumbnail, 64–1024 px ThrottlingRateLimit / ThrottlingBurstLimit 10 / 20 API request limit per second / burst AlarmEmail empty Administrator email for alerts; deploy.sh fills it from ALARM_EMAIL FailedImagesThreshold 3 Failed images within 5 minutes that trigger the alarm To change the other parameters, edit their Default in the template or pass --parameter-overrides to aws cloudformation deploy.
After deployment, the Outputs tab lists what you need:
Output Used for WebsiteUrl The HTTPS CloudFront address of the web page (the production link) ApiUrl The API Invoke URL, written into config.js DistributionId Cache invalidation after uploading a new page ImagesBucketName, WebBucketName, TableName Finding the resources in the console ApiFunctionName, ThumbnailFunctionName Logs and monitoring in Lambda / CloudWatch AlarmTopicArn Adding another administrator to the alerts A circular dependency to solve The bucket’s trigger needs the function, the function’s permission needs the bucket’s ARN, and the function’s IAM policy also needs the bucket. Referencing the bucket resource from both would create a cycle CloudFormation refuses. The template breaks it by building the bucket name from the stack name: ${AWS::StackName}-images-${AWS::AccountId}-${AWS::Region}. The permission and the policy use that string, not a reference to the bucket.
Deploy with one command Download snapthumb.zip. In CloudShell choose Actions → Upload file, upload it, then run:
unzip -oq snapthumb.zip && cd snapthumb export ALARM_EMAIL=you@example.com # optional: receive alarm emails bash deploy.sh Verified on a real account (ap-southeast-1, 18/11/2026): the template created all 18 resources on the first attempt (table, 2 buckets + policy, 2 functions, 2 roles, 2 log groups, 2 permissions, HTTP API, integration, 3 routes, stage) in about 1–2 minutes. Adding the alerts on 22/11/2026 (SNS topic, email subscription, metric filter and 3 alarms) brought the stack to 24 resources. Adding CloudFront the same day (Origin Access Control and distribution) brought it to 26; the first deployment now takes about 5–8 minutes because the distribution has to reach every edge location.
deploy.sh runs four steps: create or update the stack; package the Thumbnail function with Pillow; upload both functions’ code; upload the web page with config.js filled in and clear the CloudFront cache (invalidation /*). It prints the HTTPS CloudFront address at the end.
Automated tests backend/test_app.py runs the whole flow against mocked AWS (moto): create an upload link, upload, run the thumbnail handler, list, delete, plus broken files, transparent PNGs, portrait and small images, and invalid input. Two regression tests cover images uploaded straight to S3 and records without file keys.
Run the tests on your computer or in CloudShell:
pip install "moto[s3,dynamodb]" Pillow cd backend && python3 -m unittest -v

title: Clean Up Resources
content:
If you built by hand (5.3–5.7) CloudFront: select the distribution → Disable, wait until it shows Disabled (a few minutes), then Delete. Then Security → Origin access → delete the OAC. API Gateway: delete snapthumb-api. Lambda: delete snapthumb-api and snapthumb-thumbnail; Layers: delete pillow-py312. CloudWatch → Log groups: delete /aws/lambda/snapthumb-api and /aws/lambda/snapthumb-thumbnail. DynamoDB: delete snapthumb-images. S3: Empty then Delete snapthumb-images-… and snapthumb-web-…. IAM → Roles: delete the roles starting with snapthumb-api-role and snapthumb-thumbnail-role. CloudWatch → Alarms: delete the three snapthumb-… alarms; Amazon SNS: delete the topic snapthumb-alarms and its subscription. (The metric filter is deleted with its log group.) If you used CloudFormation (5.9) cd ~/snapthumb && bash destroy.sh Type yes; the script empties both buckets and deletes the stack. Deleting the stack also removes the CloudFront distribution and its OAC, the three alarms, the SNS topic and its subscription, the metric filter, both Lambda functions, the API, the table, the IAM roles and the log groups.
If you also published the Pillow layer in 5.5.1, delete it as well: Lambda → Layers → pillow-py312 → Delete for each version. Layers are not part of the stack.
The monthly budget from 5.2 can stay as a safety net; delete it in Billing and Cost Management → Budgets if you no longer want its emails.
Cost of leaving it running If you need to keep SnapThumb online for a while (for example until the report is graded), it costs almost nothing (the detailed estimate by usage is in Proposal, section 6):
Part Cost while idle Note Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB on-demand 0 USD Billed per request only S3 About 0.025 USD per GB per month A few test images are a few MB CloudWatch 0 USD 3 alarms and 1 custom metric fit in the Free Tier (10 alarms, 10 custom metrics); logs are kept 14 days CloudFront 0 USD The always-free tier covers 1 TB of data out and 10 million requests a month; deleting the stack takes 5–15 minutes longer because CloudFront must disable the distribution first SNS email 0 USD Emails are sent only when an alarm changes state Delete everything as soon as you no longer need it.
